title: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element, with every operation running in constant time.

s1_definition.profdef: A min stack is a stack that, in addition to push, pop, and top, returns the current minimum element in constant time. The standard design keeps a second stack of running minimums in lockstep with the main stack, so the top of the min stack is always the smallest value currently present. Every operation is constant time because each one does a fixed amount of work on both stacks.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture a clerk at the National Bank of India stacking account balance slips. Next to the main spike she keeps a second spike of "smallest-so-far" slips. Every time she adds a balance, she also adds a slip showing the smallest balance seen up to that point. When she removes the top balance, she removes the matching smallest-so-far slip too. So at any instant she can glance at the top of the second spike and instantly know the smallest balance on the stack, without scanning everything.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a parallel min-stack whose top is always the current minimum, so getMin is constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A min stack is a stack that, in addition to push, pop, and top, returns the current minimum element in constant time. The standard design keeps a second stack of running minimums in lockstep with the main stack, so the top of the min stack is always the smallest value currently present. Every operation is constant time because each one does a fixed amount of work on both stacks.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture a clerk at the National Bank of India stacking account balance slips. Next to the main spike she keeps a second spike of "smallest-so-far" slips. Every time she adds a balance, she also adds a slip showing the smallest balance seen up to that point. When she removes the top balance, she removes the matching smallest-so-far slip too. So at any instant she can glance at the top of the second spike and instantly know the smallest balance on the stack, without scanning everything.

**One line to remember:** Keep a parallel min-stack whose top is always the current minimum, so getMin is constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive way to get the minimum is to scan the whole stack, which is linear time per query and too slow when getMin is called frequently. The trick is to pay a tiny constant cost on every push and pop so that the minimum is always ready in constant time.

You maintain two `ArrayDeque` stacks, the main one and a min one. On `push(x)` you always push onto the main stack, and you push onto the min stack either x or the current minimum, whichever is smaller: `minStack.push(minStack.isEmpty() ? x : Math.min(x, minStack.peek()));`. This way the min stack top mirrors the smallest value among all elements currently in the main stack. On `pop()` you pop both stacks together so they stay aligned. On `top()` you peek the main stack, and on `getMin()` you peek the min stack.

Because money in banking uses BigDecimal, the comparison must use `compareTo` rather than the less-than operator, for example `cur.compareTo(x) <= 0 ? cur : x`. Using equals-aware comparison with `<= 0` keeps duplicates handled correctly, so if the same minimum is pushed twice, popping once still leaves the minimum available from the earlier copy.

A senior-level nuance is the space-optimised variant. Instead of storing a full min on every push, you can push onto the min stack only when a new value is less than or equal to the current minimum, and pop from it only when the popped main value equals the current minimum. That saves memory when minimums repeat rarely, at the cost of slightly trickier pop logic. Another encoding stores deltas from the minimum in a single stack, trading clarity for space. For interviews the two-stack version is the clearest correct answer, and I mention the optimisations to show depth.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A risk dashboard at the National Bank of India pushes and pops account balances as positions open and close through the day, and the desk constantly asks "what is the lowest balance currently exposed?" Scanning all open positions on every query is too slow during peak trading. We need the running minimum available instantly. This is exactly a min stack, because the answer is always the smallest value currently on the stack.

Problem 2 — Balances must be exact money values, so we cannot use primitive doubles; we use BigDecimal and compare with compareTo. The min stack must therefore track the minimum BigDecimal correctly, including when the same lowest balance appears more than once.

In our mini-project we build a `MinBalanceStack` backed by two deques of BigDecimal. The demo pushes several balances, reads the minimum, pops one, and reads the minimum again to show it updates in constant time.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: push one million, then two hundred fifty thousand, then five hundred thousand, then two pops.

Step 1: Push one million. The main stack holds one million. The min stack is empty, so it stores one million as the minimum.

Step 2: Push two hundred fifty thousand. The main stack now has it on top. The current min was one million, and two hundred fifty thousand is smaller, so the min stack pushes two hundred fifty thousand.

Step 3: Push five hundred thousand. The current min is two hundred fifty thousand, which is still smaller than five hundred thousand, so the min stack pushes two hundred fifty thousand again, keeping the minimum correct.

Step 4: We read the top, which is five hundred thousand, and the minimum, which is two hundred fifty thousand, both in constant time from the respective stack tops.

Step 5: We pop. Both stacks drop their top, removing five hundred thousand from main and the duplicated two hundred fifty thousand from the min stack. The minimum is still two hundred fifty thousand.

Step 6: We pop again, removing two hundred fifty thousand from main and its min entry. Now the main stack holds only one million, and the min stack top is one million, so the minimum correctly becomes one million.

```
[2026-10-26 23:21:01] INFO    Top balance: 500000
[2026-10-26 23:21:01] INFO    Min balance: 250000
[2026-10-26 23:21:01] INFO    After pop, min: 250000
[2026-10-26 23:21:01] INFO    After pop, min: 1000000
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Min Stack (Two-Stack Design) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Auxiliary-stack technique — parallel min invariant           │
  │  Decorator-like wrapper over Deque with extra bookkeeping     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: MinBalanceStack only manages the stack + its minimum      │
  │  O: swap compareTo for a Comparator to support other orders   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           MinBalanceStack             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - main: Deque<BigDecimal>            │  main values
  │  - mins: Deque<BigDecimal>            │  running minimums
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + push(x): void                      │  O(1)
  │  + pop(): BigDecimal                  │  O(1)
  │  + top(): BigDecimal                  │  O(1)
  │  + getMin(): BigDecimal               │  O(1)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Invariant: mins.peek() == min(main)

  ── State Diagram: Min invariant ─────────────────────────

  [push x] → mins.push(min(x, mins.peek))
  [pop]    → both stacks pop together (stay aligned)
  [getMin] → mins.peek() (never scans)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. push(x): main.push(x); mins.push(min(x, cur))
  2. pop(): mins.pop(); return main.pop()
  3. getMin(): return mins.peek()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A min stack is a stack that supports push, pop, top, and getMin all in constant time. The naive approach of scanning the stack to find the minimum is linear per query, which is too slow when getMin is called often, so instead I keep a second stack of running minimums alongside the main stack. The top of that min stack is always the smallest value currently present, so getMin is just a peek.

The mechanics are simple and that is the point. On every push I push the value onto the main stack and I push onto the min stack whichever is smaller between the new value and the current minimum. On every pop I pop both stacks together so they stay perfectly aligned. Because each operation does a fixed amount of work on two stacks, every operation is constant time, and because I store a min entry per element, the extra space is linear.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this for a risk dashboard where account balances are pushed and popped as positions open and close, and the desk constantly asks for the lowest balance currently exposed. Since the balances are money, I store them as BigDecimal and compare with compareTo rather than primitive operators, and I use a less-than-or-equal comparison so repeated minimums are handled correctly when the same lowest balance appears twice.

The senior-level point I add is that there are space optimisations. I can push to the min stack only when a value is less than or equal to the current minimum and pop from it only when the popped value equals the current minimum, which saves memory when minimums repeat rarely. There is also a delta-encoding variant that uses a single stack. I present the clean two-stack version as my default because it is obviously correct, and I mention the optimisations to show I understand the space-time trade-off.
